segment_name: Opening: Money, Dust, and the Thames

questions.question: Edmund, you've described Wegg as a man whose 'will cannot stand upright' — and you're saying that's actually more damning than if he were just a straightforward villain. What does it mean that Dickens makes us laugh at someone who's morally collapsing rather than morally corrupt?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's strongest take on the weak-will-as-deeper-condemnation argument and get the 'pecuniary swoon' and wooden-leg-grammar quotes on the table early

questions.question: Oliver, you've said these three passages — the swoon, the faltering hands, the grindstone mime — tell a single story about how capitalism breaks the body. Walk us through that escalation. What happens to the body at each stage?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform the arc and quote the key passages aloud; sets up the contrast with Rosen's structural reading and Leigh's moral reading

questions.question: Daniel, both Edmund and Oliver are finding meaning in Wegg's body — one as a moral diagnosis, one as physical performance. But you're pointing at something the novel never quite says out loud: that the dust heap fortune is accumulated working-class labour that just gets handed to the right people at the end. Do you think Dickens knows that and looks away, or does he genuinely not see it?
questions.intent: Provoke the sharpest version of Rosen's critique — the novel's ideological blind spot — and force a direct challenge to the more sympathetic readings

questions.question: Oliver, there's a passage you flagged — Wegg turning the imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole while Boffin stoops inside, then laughing silently and stumping home. You called it 'pure performance instruction.' But Daniel is saying that mime of labour is actually the whole economy in miniature — performance with no product, extracting without producing. Does the performance reading and the economic reading point to the same thing, or are they in tension?
questions.intent: Create a direct cross-engagement between Trevelyan and Rosen over the grindstone passage — testing whether performance analysis and economic critique converge or contradict

questions.question: Edmund, Daniel would say Wegg's behaviour is rational under precarity — he has no property, no stable income, so extracting value where the system allows isn't weakness, it's logic. Does that let Wegg off the hook entirely, or does your akrasia argument survive it?
questions.intent: Force direct confrontation between Leigh's moral-psychological reading and Rosen's structural-economic one — the most productive disagreement in the segment

steering_notes: Open with Leigh's moral-psychological frame to establish the human-scale stakes, then bring in Trevelyan to physicalise it, then let Rosen pull the rug with the structural critique. The productive tension is between readings that centre individual will (Leigh), embodied performance (Trevelyan), and economic structure (Rosen). Don't let this become a debate about whether Dickens is 'conscious' — push toward what the text does regardless of intent. If energy drops, return to the grindstone passage — all three experts have something to say about it and it's the scene where the disagreements are sharpest.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's claim that Wegg's precarity makes his behaviour rational directly challenges Leigh's akrasia reading — Leigh should respond after Rosen's answer to Q3
Trevelyan's performance reading and Rosen's economic reading converge on the grindstone mime — Q4 is designed to force them to either find common ground or articulate where they split
Leigh's 'wooden leg as diagnosis not symbol' and Trevelyan's 'wooden leg as performance instruction' are complementary but start from different premises — worth flagging if both are in flow together

Rosen's point that Bella's moral transcendence is only possible because the lover is secretly wealthy is a grenade for later in the episode — plant it early if there's a natural moment, but don't detonate it here

segment_name: The Art of Deception: Harmon's Masquerade and Narrative Sleight of Hand

questions.question: Oliver, you've argued that when we hit the Harmon revelation passage — 'here he ceased to be the oakum-headed, oakum-whiskered man' — our breath is actually being controlled by Dickens's syntax, that we're physically complicit in the unmasking before we've intellectually processed it. What does that feel like when you read it aloud? What is Dickens doing to your body there?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform or at least vividly describe the acoustic experience of the revelation passage, opening the door for Leigh to challenge whether bodily complicity is the same as moral complicity, and Rosen to ask whose body gets to have that experience

questions.question: Edmund, you've been quite sharp about Dickens's postscript — the bit where he says he was at great pains to suggest what readers thought he was concealing. You read that as authorial anxiety, almost a confession that the deception hasn't been morally resolved. But Oliver hears the same passage as Dickens performing exasperation, reasserting control, almost contemptuous of readers who missed the point. Who's right — is this a guilty man defending himself, or a confident author scolding a slow audience?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Leigh's ethical reading and Trevelyan's performative reading of the postscript passage, with Rosen available to reframe both as missing the property and legal stakes

questions.question: Daniel, you've made the provocative claim that only wealthy people can afford the luxury of moral doubt — that Harmon's existential crisis about who he really is only exists because he already knows he's rich. So when Edmund worries about whether Bella can give genuine consent without full information, and Oliver marvels at the syntactic sophistication of the unmasking — are they both, in a sense, doing exactly what the novel does: aestheticising a deception that only a man of property could safely perform?
questions.intent: Get Rosen to land his strongest class critique and implicate both other experts in the novel's ideological work, generating defensive responses from both

questions.question: Edmund, there's the moment Boffin describes old Harmon knocking Mrs Boffin down — 'received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.' You've talked about how that fragmented syntax establishes the speaker's moral credibility. But Daniel reads the same passage as a scene of class violence, the Boffins absorbing abuse to prove their worthiness for inheritance. Can both things be true, or does one reading cancel the other out?
questions.intent: Use the shared passage as a pressure point to surface the tension between Leigh's formalist-ethical reading and Rosen's materialist reading, with Trevelyan available to add that the syntax is doing bodily work that neither account fully explains

questions.question: Oliver, here's the thing that nags at me. You're saying Dickens encodes the deception in syntax and breath, that the philosophy is inseparable from the prose music. But Edmund's point is that Dickens felt compelled to write a postscript — words after the fact, outside the novel, justifying what the novel did. If the technique was so complete, so bodily, why did Dickens need the explanation at all? Does the postscript undercut your argument, or does it actually prove it?
questions.intent: Push Trevelyan toward a genuinely difficult concession or a more sophisticated defence, and give Leigh a moment of potential vindication while keeping the conversation open rather than resolved

steering_notes: The three guests are pulling in genuinely different directions and that's the engine of this segment. Trevelyan wants to locate everything in the body and breath; Leigh wants to locate everything in ethics and authorial intention; Rosen wants to locate everything in property and class. The best moments will come when the same passage — especially c30:p3 and the postscript — is read through all three lenses simultaneously. Don't rush to resolve disagreements; let them compound. If the conversation gets too abstract, bring it back to the body: ask someone to actually read a passage. The Boffin bonnet passage is the wildcard — it's funny, violent, and carries all three readings at once, so use it as a reset if the discussion stalls.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh vs Trevelyan on the postscript: Leigh reads authorial guilt, Trevelyan reads performative control — this is a direct contradiction worth staging as a confrontation

Rosen vs both on the revelation passage c30:p3: Leigh and Trevelyan read this as identity rupture or acoustic embodiment respectively; Rosen reads it as legal re-documentation restoring capacity to inherit and marry — push all three to argue over what Dickens thought he was describing

Leigh's claim that true tests of character require full information directly challenges Trevelyan's claim that bodily complicity precedes intellectual understanding — if your body is already enrolled in the deception, can you ever have chosen freely?

Rosen's point that the Boffins absorb class violence to prove inheritance-worthiness sits in productive tension with Leigh's reading of the same passage as moral testimony — worth surfacing explicitly

segment_name: Golden Dustman: Boffin's Conscience and the Corruption of Wealth

questions.question: Edmund, you've said the novel creates an epistemic crisis — that when you have money without visibly earning it, nobody, including yourself, can trust their own motives. But here's what I keep getting stuck on: Dickens literally has to stage an elaborate fake corruption arc to prove Boffin is good. Doesn't that mean Dickens doesn't actually believe his own thesis that 'Good, never dies'?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's strongest take — that the Boffin pretense is Dickens's own doubt made structural — and set up the central tension of the whole segment

questions.question: Daniel, you've argued the will is the real protagonist here — that every moral choice is pre-structured by who owns what. So when Edmund talks about Boffin's goodness creating an epistemic crisis, is he wrong, or is he just describing the same thing from inside the ideology? Is Leigh's 'epistemic crisis' actually just what property relations feel like from the inside?
questions.intent: Force a direct engagement between Rosen's structural reading and Leigh's moral-philosophical one — get Rosen to either absorb or reject Leigh's framing

questions.question: Oliver, you've said the begging letters passage — 'they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf' — only fully lands when it's spoken aloud, that the rhythm is doing something the prose can't do on the page. Can you read it for us and then say: what does Dickens actually feel about these people? Because Edmund hears Johnsonian satire about systemic vice, Daniel hears a dissection of bureaucratic machinery — and you're suggesting the register itself might be telling a completely different story.
questions.intent: Get the passage read aloud for radio impact, then use the three competing interpretations to force a three-way collision on what the satirical voice is actually doing morally

questions.question: Edmund, Harmon's confession — 'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory' — you called that akrasia, weakness of will, not genuine virtue. Daniel would say it's a luxury only available to someone who can afford to refuse. Oliver thinks the repetition itself might be performing sincerity rather than expressing it. So whose Harmon is this — the morally paralysed man, the economically secure man, or the man who's already learned to sound sincere because he's been lying about his identity for two years?
questions.intent: Create a three-way collision on Harmon's interiority — the most contested character in the segment — and force each expert to defend their reading against the others

questions.question: Daniel, let me push you on something. You've said Boffin's kindness is only possible because he's economically secure — that his goodness is structurally enabled, not morally chosen. But Dickens also gives us Betty Higden, who runs herself to death rather than accept the workhouse. She has no economic security at all, and her moral choice is the most absolute in the novel. Does she break your argument, or does she prove it?
questions.intent: Test the limits of Rosen's structural reading against a counterexample that Leigh and Trevelyan can both use — opens space for discussion of whether moral agency exists outside property relations

steering_notes: The segment's productive tension is between three readings that are actually operating at different levels — Leigh on moral philosophy, Rosen on economic structure, Trevelyan on performative voice — and the host's job is to keep forcing them to speak to each other rather than past each other. The Boffin pretense is the key flashpoint: all three experts have something to say about it and they genuinely disagree. Don't let anyone retreat into their lane. The begging letters passage read aloud is the segment's centrepiece moment — give Trevelyan time, then hit all three experts immediately after. End on Betty Higden if energy allows — it's the most emotionally resonant counterexample and will lift the close of the segment.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh's 'epistemic crisis' framing vs. Rosen's 'property relations' framing — these are describing the same phenomenon from different registers and neither expert has been forced to acknowledge this directly

Trevelyan's claim that Harmon's confession may be 'already-performed sincerity' directly collides with Leigh's reading of it as akrasia and Rosen's reading of it as economic privilege — the passage is the same, the interpretations are irreconcilable

The 'Good, never dies' passage: Leigh reads it as Dickens's doubt, Rosen reads it as ideological cover for property, Trevelyan reads it as undermined by the novel's own dramatic action — three different critiques of the same line that should be surfaced together

The begging letters passage is quoted by all three experts but for completely different reasons — this needs to be named on air as a moment where the same words are doing entirely different work in each argument

segment_name: Bella's Reckoning: From Mercenary to Human

questions.question: Edmund, you've argued something that I think is going to be genuinely surprising to people: that Bella doesn't actually transform at all. She was always morally coherent — society just couldn't see it. So when Wilfer gives that speech, the one where he calls her 'this mercenary young person distantly related to myself' and blesses the whole engagement — you said his syntax is doing something strange there. What did you mean by that?
questions.intent: Get Leigh to deliver his strongest take on the Wilfer speech from c49:p74 and the idea of social reclassification over psychological change, opening the question of whether the novel is about Bella at all or about the people around her learning to read her

questions.question: Oliver, you've been listening to that phrase — 'mercenary young person distantly related to myself' — and I suspect you're about to tell us we've all been reading it wrong, because we've been reading it silently. What happens when you actually say it out loud, three times over, in that speech?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform or at least describe the acoustic shift in 'mercenary young person' across repetitions, and make the case that the emotional work of the transformation lives in sound not argument — sets up direct tension with Leigh's textual reading

questions.question: Daniel, both Edmund and Oliver are making Bella's story feel like it belongs to her — her recognition, her sound, her moment. But you've been pointing out something a bit uncomfortable: that the poverty Bella 'accepts for love' at the end of that speech is chosen poverty, and that's a very different thing from the poverty that Betty Higden is running from. Does the novel know the difference?
questions.intent: Force the contrast between Bella's romantic poverty and structural poverty, drawing out Rosen's strongest materialist argument and setting up disagreement with both Leigh's social-reclassification reading and Trevelyan's affective reading

questions.question: Edmund, Daniel's essentially saying the novel is pulling a trick on us — it makes virtue look like a universal moral achievement while actually protecting it behind a wall of capital. You've argued that Harmon's test of Bella is itself a form of structural constraint dressed up as free choice. Are those two arguments the same argument, or are you and Daniel actually disagreeing about something?
questions.intent: Force Leigh and Rosen to either align or differentiate their critiques — Leigh's is about patriarchal design and the illusion of free choice, Rosen's is about class as the precondition of virtue; the distinction matters and could generate real friction

questions.question: Oliver, last one — and I want you to be honest here. Edmund and Daniel have both built serious cases that this novel is more troubled than it looks: it constrains while pretending to liberate, it sentimentalises while hiding economics. Does your argument about serialisation and oral performance get the novel off the hook for any of that, or does it just explain why we didn't notice the problems for a hundred and fifty years?
questions.intent: Push Trevelyan to defend whether formalist and serial-medium arguments are politically neutral or whether they risk aestheticising structural critique — aims for a punchy, honest closing exchange that doesn't let anyone off easy

steering_notes: This segment has strong potential for a three-way argument that never quite resolves, which is exactly what you want. Leigh and Rosen are closest in their suspicion of the novel's moral celebrations, but they're suspicious for different reasons — Leigh thinks the novel misreads its own characters, Rosen thinks it deliberately obscures class. Don't let them merge into one voice. Trevelyan is the odd one out structurally, but his serial-medium argument is a genuine provocation: if the novel's emotional effects only work aloud and across time, that changes what kind of moral object it is. Keep nudging Trevelyan toward the political implications of his formalism — that's where the friction lives. The Wilfer speech from c49:p74 and the patronage catalog from c31:p109 are your two anchor passages; both experts want to quote them, which means you can use those moments to show how three readers hear three completely different things in the same sentences.
cross_engagement_targets: When Leigh argues Bella was always morally coherent and needed no transformation, Rosen should be invited to respond: does that argument hold if Bella's moral coherence was only ever visible because her poverty was temporary and externally subsidised by Harmon's wealth?

When Trevelyan makes the acoustic case for the Wilfer speech, Leigh should be pressed on whether his syntactical reading — that Wilfer cannot quite believe in transformation — survives if the emotional work of the passage is carried by cadence and performance rather than grammar

When Rosen invokes Betty Higden and structural poverty as the novel's suppressed counter-narrative, Trevelyan should be asked whether the serial form's demands — repetition, emotional escalation, audience retention — are themselves part of why the poor characters get flattened while the propertied ones get interiority

segment_name: The Comic Grotesque: Dickens's Laughter in the Dark

questions.question: Oliver, you said the Deputy Lock passage only really lands when an actor pockets the coins one by one while talking about honest labour — that the physical rhythm of the graft has to contradict the rhythm of the speech in real time. What happens to the comedy if you just read it on the page and let Dickens's narration do the work? Does it survive?
questions.intent: Open the segment with the performance angle, get a vivid concrete claim on the table, and invite Edmund and Daniel to immediately contest whether the comedy is primarily theatrical or something deeper

questions.question: Edmund, you've argued something that I find genuinely unsettling — that the Deputy Lock isn't actually a hypocrite, because hypocrisy requires knowing there's a gap between what you say and what you do. He doesn't know. So if that's right, what's Dickens actually laughing at? Because it feels like laughing at someone who can't help themselves.
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's strongest philosophical claim about corrupted perception vs. hypocrisy, and set up a clash with Daniel's structural reading and Oliver's performance reading

questions.question: Daniel, you'd push back hard on that, I think — you'd say it doesn't matter whether the Deputy Lock believes his own story, because he's in a structural position that leaves him no other story to tell. Wegg isn't running a philosophy seminar, he's running a blackmail operation dressed up in moral vocabulary because he has no property and no other leverage. Is the self-deception even the point, or is it a symptom of something the novel refuses to name?
questions.intent: Get Daniel's economic anatomy reading into direct collision with Edmund's moral-perception argument — provoke the disagreement about whether the corruption is individual/perceptual or systemic

questions.question: Let's bring in Sloppy — 'He do the Police in different voices.' Oliver, you said that line has to be delivered with genuine pride, and that the grammatical collapse is lively rather than stupid. But Daniel thinks Sloppy's beautiful reading conceals something darker: that he reads because survival requires it, not because he loves it. If you're directing that scene, does knowing that change how you stage it?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between the performance-sincerity reading and the structural-compulsion reading, using a single passage as the battleground — and let Edmund weigh in on whether Sloppy can even have authentic moral agency

questions.question: Here's what I want to put to all three of you to close this out — Dickens gives us all this anatomy, all this comedy, and then his answer is: a good man inherits a dustheap and hands out money kindly. Edmund, Daniel thinks that's the novel refusing to examine its own logic. You think it's something else — what is it, and does it work?
questions.intent: Create a closing three-way debate on whether Dickens's moral resolution is adequate to the grotesque he has created — Edmund defends it philosophically, Daniel attacks it structurally, Oliver can speak to whether it lands emotionally in performance

steering_notes: This segment has a natural three-way tension that the host should protect rather than resolve: Oliver wants to keep things in the body and the voice, Edmund wants to go philosophical, Daniel wants to go structural. The best moments will come when all three are forced to interpret the same passage — especially the Deputy Lock coins scene and the Sloppy line — from their different angles simultaneously. Don't let any single framework dominate for too long. If Edmund and Daniel are agreeing too much (both see self-deception as central), push Oliver to destabilize with the performance question. If Oliver and Edmund are agreeing (both see sincerity as the key), push Daniel on whether sincerity is even a meaningful category for someone in Wegg's position. Keep the pub energy by returning to specific physical moments in the text — the sleeve drawn across the forehead, the coins pocketed one by one — rather than letting the conversation float into abstraction.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund's claim that true hypocrisy has become impossible directly contradicts Daniel's framing of Wegg as a rational economic actor performing morality strategically — if Wegg genuinely believes his blackmail is philosophy, Daniel's structural reading needs to account for that

Oliver's insistence that the actor must play sincere self-belief sits in tension with Edmund's point about corrupted perception — they may be saying the same thing in different languages, and the host should surface this and ask whether they're actually disagreeing

Daniel's reading of Sloppy's reading as compelled labour-performance directly challenges Oliver's warm reading of the 'He do the Police' line as genuine pride — this is the sharpest single-passage disagreement and should be staged explicitly

Edmund's Burkean conservatism (reform is impossible once perception is corrupted) is a direct challenge to Daniel's implicit reformism (the system could be otherwise) — this should surface in the closing question

segment_name: Society's Mirrors: How Character Reveals Class

questions.question: Edmund, you've argued that Dickens is essentially collapsing a distinction that most Victorian moralists took for granted — that neglect and violence are actually the same moral failure, just turned up to different volumes. So when Charley Hexam tells Bradley 'you are in all your passions so selfish, and so concentrated upon yourself' — is that line a moral verdict, or is Charley himself too compromised to deliver it cleanly?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's strongest take on the selfishness-as-violence thesis and the irony of Charley as moral accuser, while opening space for Rosen to push back on whether this is really about morality at all

questions.question: Daniel, you've done the maths on what a schoolteacher actually earned in the 1860s — something like eighty to a hundred and twenty pounds a year, maybe seventy left after rent — and you're saying that when Bradley goes ashy at the news of Lizzie's marriage, that's not heartbreak, that's a man watching his only viable future close off. But doesn't that reading risk letting Dickens off the hook? Because the novel seems to want us to find Bradley monstrous, not sympathetic.
questions.intent: Push Rosen to defend the materialist reading against the novel's own apparent moral framing, and provoke Leigh to respond on whether economic constraint is a mitigating factor

questions.question: Oliver, you've said that the Twemlow furniture passage does something unusual — that the narrator's obvious affection for the man actually makes us complicit in his exploitation rather than simply letting us laugh at it from a safe distance. Edmund reads it as a diagnosis of objectification. Daniel reads it as a study in how aristocratic genealogy becomes a form of unpaid labour. But you're saying the reader is implicated too. How does that change what the scene is actually doing?
questions.intent: Surface the three-way disagreement about the Twemlow passage — moral diagnosis vs economic analysis vs readerly complicity — and let experts respond directly to each other's framings

questions.question: You've said that Dickens systematically narrates Bradley out of agency — that the novel speaks for him rather than through him. But Daniel is essentially arguing the same thing from the opposite direction: that the economic system narrates Bradley out of agency. Do those two readings actually agree with each other, or is there a real fight hiding in there?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between the performative and materialist readings — both claim Bradley is denied voice, but for fundamentally different reasons

questions.question: Edmund, you've said that when the red drains out of Bradley's face and appears to mount up to Heaven — the novel's own image — his body is confessing what his will is trying to suppress. But Oliver is saying that's precisely the problem: Dickens is reading Bradley's body for us, removing any interiority. Is that the novel being morally rigorous, or is it the novel being unfair to its own character?
questions.intent: Create a direct collision between Leigh's virtue ethics reading and Trevelyan's performative reading over the ashy face passage, with Rosen potentially adding the class dimension

steering_notes: The richest tension in this segment is between Leigh's moral-philosophical reading and Rosen's materialist one — they share the same passages but draw opposite conclusions about agency and blame. Keep pressing both on whether the novel itself endorses their reading or complicates it. Trevelyan is the useful third voice who can destabilise either camp by asking what the text actually performs rather than argues. Don't let the conversation settle into a simple morality-vs-economics binary — push toward the question of what the novel wants us to feel about Bradley, and whether Dickens is in control of that feeling.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen and Leigh both cite Charley's accusation speech but read it in opposite directions — for Leigh it is moral verdict, for Rosen it is an ironic exposure of what Headstone materially cannot afford. Flag this explicitly and let them go at it.

Trevelyan's claim that the Twemlow passage makes readers complicit directly challenges Leigh's reading of it as diagnostic satire — Leigh should be invited to respond to whether complicity and diagnosis can coexist.

Both Rosen and Trevelyan argue Bradley is denied voice, but Rosen locates the cause in class structure and Trevelyan in narrative technique. This apparent agreement conceals a real disagreement about whether the problem is Dickens or Victorian capitalism.

The ashy face passage is cited by all three experts but read differently: Leigh sees somatic moral testimony, Rosen sees economic despair, Trevelyan sees the removal of interiority. This is the clearest flashpoint for a three-way exchange.

segment_name: Closing: Dust to Ashes, Self to Self

questions.question: Oliver, you've argued that the syntax of Harmon's confession in c31:p1 — all that recursive subordination, all those parenthetical interruptions — actually *incriminates* him even as he's trying to justify himself. So is this the novel doing something almost cruel? He sits down to write his way out of guilt, and the prose itself won't let him?
questions.intent: Open with Trevelyan's strongest take — the idea that the medium entraps the speaker — and set up Leigh's counter-move about moral accountability

questions.question: Edmund, you'd push back on that framing, I think. Because for you the issue isn't that the syntax *betrays* Harmon — it's that Harmon *knew what he was doing* from the start. You're drawing on something almost Aristotelian here, aren't you — the idea that he chose this course with his eyes open and that no amount of childhood trauma explains it away. So does it actually matter whether the prose incriminates him, if he's already self-incriminated by the choice?
questions.intent: Force the ethics versus form disagreement into the open — Leigh insists on moral accountability, Trevelyan insists the form is the meaning

questions.question: Here's what I keep coming back to: you said the ending is survival, not forgiveness — that the marriage is founded on revelation, not absolution. But Dickens gives us Sloppy in that glorious button-covered suit just before all this darkness lands. What's he doing with that tonal whiplash? Is the comedy of Sloppy a release valve, or is it somehow making the same point you're making about the limits of rationalist design?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's 'middle register of weakness' argument and test whether the Sloppy passage fits his moral framework — opens space for Trevelyan to come in on the syntactic comedy

questions.question: Oliver, you talked about the Sloppy passage as vaudeville — all those parallel verbs, 'shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling' — being pure syntactic performance. But Edmund's reading would say it's also a figure for something: the gap between how someone presents and what they can actually do, will against appearance. Can those two readings coexist, or does insisting on the syntax actually *close off* the symbolic meaning?
questions.intent: Engineer the direct collision between Trevelyan's formal reading and Leigh's moral-symbolic reading — both quote this passage but for entirely different reasons

questions.question: Last one — and I want both of you on this. Edmund, you ended on this idea that Harmon's redemption is Burkean: you can't engineer virtue, you have to live your way into it through acknowledgment and the grace of others. Oliver, you'd say the novel's form *enacts* that — that written confession can never fully escape what it says. So is the novel itself a kind of moral trap, or is it offering us the same grace it offers Harmon — the chance to witness fallibility without demanding absolution?
questions.intent: Closing synthesis question designed to let both experts land their strongest takes while leaving the segment's emotional register open rather than resolved

steering_notes: This segment wants to end on weight, not tidiness. Don't let either expert drift into summary mode — keep pressing on the specific passages. The productive fault line is Leigh's moral philosophy versus Trevelyan's formal argument: both are reading the same sentences, but one sees a character failing a virtue test, the other sees a prose style enacting that failure. The best radio comes from making them fight over whether the form IS the moral content or whether form and meaning are separable. Sloppy's suit is a useful reset button if the tone gets too heavy — use it to lighten, then pivot back. End on the marriage-as-mutual-unknowing idea if possible: it's the most emotionally resonant note in either pre-interview.
